# Multiple dispatch {#sec-multiple-dispatch}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

Most S3 generics choose a method from the class of one argument, usually the first. This is called *single dispatch*. S3's operators check both operands for a method (@sec-operators), but each method still belongs to a single class. S4 and S7 can choose a method from the classes of several arguments together, which is called *multiple dispatch*. It suits operations where the answer depends on both inputs. The sum of two independent normal variables is normal; a normal plus a constant is a shifted normal; a normal plus a uniform is no standard distribution at all, though its mean and variance still follow from those of the two inputs. This chapter writes that operation with S4 methods and with Rust traits, and then shows where Rust's compile-time approach stops and R's runtime approach keeps going. The matching section of the Rust book is "Advanced Traits", which covers associated types, such as `Add`'s `Output`, and operator overloading [@rustbook, sec. 20.2].

## Methods for pairs of classes in S4

S4 methods can be defined for a *signature*, the classes of several arguments together. Here are the classes involved. The two that a sum can return, `Normal` and `Moments`, get compact `show()` methods like those in @sec-display:

```{r}
#| label: r-s4-classes
setClass("Normal", slots = c(mean = "numeric", sd = "numeric"))
setClass("Uniform", slots = c(min = "numeric", max = "numeric"))
setClass("Moments", slots = c(mean = "numeric", variance = "numeric"))

setMethod("show", "Normal", function(object) {
  cat("Normal(mean = ", object@mean, ", sd = ", object@sd, ")\n", sep = "")
})
setMethod("show", "Moments", function(object) {
  cat("Moments(mean = ", object@mean,
      ", variance = ", object@variance, ")\n", sep = "")
})
```

A `Moments` object holds a mean and a variance, the answer when the sum isn't a named distribution. Each pair of classes then gets its own method for `+`:

```{r}
#| label: r-s4-plus
setMethod("+", signature("Normal", "Normal"), function(e1, e2) {
  new("Normal", mean = e1@mean + e2@mean, sd = sqrt(e1@sd^2 + e2@sd^2))
})

setMethod("+", signature("Normal", "numeric"), function(e1, e2) {
  new("Normal", mean = e1@mean + e2, sd = e1@sd)
})

setMethod("+", signature("Normal", "Uniform"), function(e1, e2) {
  new("Moments",
      mean = e1@mean + (e2@min + e2@max) / 2,
      variance = e1@sd^2 + (e2@max - e2@min)^2 / 12)
})

n <- new("Normal", mean = 0, sd = 3)
u <- new("Uniform", min = 0, max = 6)
n + n
n + 5
n + u
```

R looked at both operands to pick each method. Order matters, because a signature lists its classes by position. No method covers `Uniform` plus `Normal`, so R falls back to the built-in `+`, which can't add two S4 objects:

```{r}
#| label: r-s4-plus-missing
#| error: true
u + n
```

## Implementations for pairs of types in Rust

In Rust, each pair is an implementation of `Add`, with the right-hand type as the trait's type parameter, as in @sec-operators. The `Output` type differs from pair to pair:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-add-pairs
use std::ops::Add;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Uniform {
    min: f64,
    max: f64,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Moments {
    mean: f64,
    variance: f64,
}

impl Add<Normal> for Normal {
    type Output = Normal;

    fn add(self, other: Normal) -> Normal {
        Normal {
            mean: self.mean + other.mean,
            sd: (self.sd * self.sd + other.sd * other.sd).sqrt(),
        }
    }
}

impl Add<f64> for Normal {
    type Output = Normal;

    fn add(self, shift: f64) -> Normal {
        Normal { mean: self.mean + shift, sd: self.sd }
    }
}

impl Add<Uniform> for Normal {
    type Output = Moments;

    fn add(self, other: Uniform) -> Moments {
        Moments {
            mean: self.mean + (other.min + other.max) / 2.0,
            variance: self.sd * self.sd
                + (other.max - other.min).powi(2) / 12.0,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let n = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 3.0 };
    let u = Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 };
    println!("{:?}", n + n);
    println!("{:?}", n + 5.0);
    println!("{:?}", n + u);
}
```

The three implementations correspond one to one with the three S4 methods, and order matters here too: `u + n` doesn't compile, because nothing implements `Add<Normal> for Uniform`. Where R picked each method when `+` ran, the compiler picked each implementation from the operand types. It also knows each result's type, so code that receives `n + u` knows it has `Moments` and not a `Normal`, without checking.

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
An S4 signature such as `signature("Normal", "Uniform")` and the Rust header `impl Add<Uniform> for Normal` say the same thing: this code handles a `Normal` on the left and a `Uniform` on the right. For operations where the types are known when the code is written, the two approaches line up closely.
:::

## Types known only at runtime

The two approaches part ways when the types aren't known until the program runs. Here's a list of normals, summed pairwise with `Reduce()`:

```{r}
#| label: r-reduce
dists <- list(n, new("Normal", mean = 1, sd = 4), n)
Reduce(`+`, dists)
```

R chose a method for each addition from the classes of the values at that moment. If the list held a mix of normals and uniforms, it would still pick the right method for each pair, or fail on a pair with no method, at runtime. Rust can't do that with the code above. Its implementations are chosen from types the compiler knows, and a list of mixed distributions, which @sec-generics builds, has a single type for all of its elements. The compiler can't choose an implementation from what each element turns out to be when the program runs.

S4 also handles general cases. A method for `signature("Distribution", "Distribution")`, using the virtual class from @sec-s4, would catch every pair of distributions that has no more specific method, and S4 picks the closest match. Rust has no direct counterpart. An `Add` implementation open on both sides, any distribution plus any distribution, breaks the orphan rule from @sec-s3-traits, because the type on the left could come from another crate. With `Normal` on the left, a generic implementation for any distribution on the right compiles, but not alongside the specific `Add<Normal> for Normal`, which it overlaps. The compiler rejects the pair (@sec-generics shows the error).

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
Multiple dispatch on runtime classes has no direct equivalent in Rust. When you need it, there are two workarounds:

- **Use only the shared interface.** Means and variances add for any pair of independent variables, so a function that takes any two distributions and calls only trait methods covers every pair at once. The next section writes it for types the compiler knows, and @sec-generics shows the form that takes distributions chosen at runtime.
- **Use an enum.** If the set of distributions is fixed, an enum holds any of them, and a `match` on a pair of enum values chooses the code for each combination at runtime. @sec-enums shows how.
:::

## Using the shared interface

When the answer only needs what every distribution provides, multiple dispatch isn't needed. Means and variances add for independent variables, so one function covers every pair, using the `Distribution` trait from @sec-s3-traits (compiled but not shown here):

```{rust}
#| label: rust-sum-moments
# trait Distribution {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64;
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64;
# }
#
# #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
# struct Normal {
#     mean: f64,
#     sd: f64,
# }
#
# impl Distribution for Normal {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
#         self.mean
#     }
#
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
#         self.sd * self.sd
#     }
# }
#
# #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
# struct Uniform {
#     min: f64,
#     max: f64,
# }
#
# impl Distribution for Uniform {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
#         (self.min + self.max) / 2.0
#     }
#
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
#         (self.max - self.min).powi(2) / 12.0
#     }
# }
#
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Moments {
    mean: f64,
    variance: f64,
}

fn sum_moments(a: impl Distribution, b: impl Distribution) -> Moments {
    Moments {
        mean: a.mean() + b.mean(),
        variance: a.variance() + b.variance(),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let n = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 3.0 };
    let u = Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 };
    println!("{:?}", sum_moments(n, u));
}
```

The function `sum_moments()` works for both orders and for any distribution added later, because it relies only on `mean()` and `variance()`. What it gives up is the specific answer: two normals produce `Moments`, not a `Normal`. That's the tradeoff. Where the calculation and the result's type differ from pair to pair, as in the three additions, each pair needs its own implementation. Where every pair can share one calculation and one result type, a function using the shared trait is simpler than any dispatch.

As written, `sum_moments()` still needs argument types the compiler knows. To accept the elements of a mixed list, its arguments become trait objects, which @sec-generics introduces.

S7, R's newest object system, also supports multiple dispatch, with methods registered for a list of classes; @sec-s7 shows it.

## Summary

| R (S4) | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `setMethod("+", signature("Normal", "Uniform"), ...)` | `impl Add<Uniform> for Normal` |
| Each method can return any class | Each `impl` names its `Output` type |
| A missing pair fails when called | A missing pair doesn't compile |
| Methods are chosen from runtime classes | Implementations are chosen from compile-time types |
| A method for `("Distribution", "Distribution")` catches the rest | Overlapping general and specific implementations are rejected |
| Mixed lists dispatch per element | An enum and `match`, or trait objects that use only the shared trait |
